newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia budget row looms, Yeltsin, ex-aide to speak.
newsitem.headline: Russia budget row looms, Yeltsin, ex-aide to speak.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will speak on Russian radio on Friday as his government's budget faces almost certain defeat in parliament amid growing discontent with deep spending cuts in the public sector.

Yeltsin, whose second radio talk in eight days is due on air at 0700 GMT, may, Kremlin sources say, address wage arrears that have forced groups ranging from industrial workers to teachers and luminaries of the arts and sciences onto the streets.
On Thursday, the 65-year-old leader met his chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, where he is preparing for heart bypass surgery.
Looking relaxed in brief television shots, he told Chubais big business tax dodgers meant problems with state spending.

"Students, teachers, the military and other workers in the state sphere are not receiving wages because a number of big enterprises are literally taking the finances of the country by the throat and refusing to pay taxes," Yeltsin said.

That is unlikely to appease his Communist opponents, who dominate the State Duma and are set to lead demands that the government revise its austere 1997 budget, which has its first reading in the lower house of parliament on Friday.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said the government was breaking promises Yeltsin made during his reelection campaign.
"The budget doesn't correspond to those main messages which were in the (government) statement when (parliament) confirmed its appointment," said Zyuganov, the runner-up in July's vote.

Legislators said the budget is virtually certain to be rejected. The Communists and their close allies have over 200 of the Duma's 450 seats. Even the party set up by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Our Home is Russia, wants it reviewed.
After warnings of an army mutiny from Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed, Chernomyrdin has already said he will look for more money for the military.
But the queue for cash does not end there, leaving the government trying to make ends meet to keep its promises to the International Monetary Fund, which helps bankroll any shortfall.

The bill targets the 1997 budget deficit at 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, down from 3.85 percent planned for this year. Ministers agree it is tight but say it will deliver lower interest rates and halve annual inflation to about 10 percent.
A compromise is likely to be reached on the budget, however.

Under the constitution, which gives the president vast powers, Yeltsin can dissolve the Duma if it persistently votes against the government. Few opposition deputies, elected at a high tide of discontent last December, want to risk their seats.
Yeltsin's meeting with Chubais was the latest of a number of discussions with officials since he moved from a Moscow hospital last weekend. His operation is due within a couple of months.
There was no word on whether Yeltsin and Chubais discussed the jockeying for position that has been going on since the president dropped out of sight shortly before his reelection.
Friday may see a new round of mudslinging.

Alexander Korzhakov, Yeltsin's close friend and chief bodyguard who was sacked in June, is scheduled to give a news conference at 1300 GMT. An avowed enemy of Chubais, Korzhakov says he has evidence of high-level corruption.
The burly bodyguard, who has come out in support of Lebed's ambitions to succeed Yeltsin at the expense of potential rivals like Chernomyrdin, has himself been under attack, however.
The former head of the National Sports Foundation, which Russian media have called a Kremlin slush fund, accused Korzhakov on Sunday of trying to extort $40 million from him.
Analysts speculate the accusations may be a preemptive Kremlin attack on an alliance between Lebed and Korzhakov. Korzhakov said the authorities want to silence him.
